title: Nero d'Avola
description: Also called Calabrese. Sicily's signature red: dark, ripe and juicy, with fresh acidity.
L: Describe Nero d'Avola's flavours and structure

Nero d'Avola means the black of Avola, a town in south-east Sicily. It gives deeply coloured wines with black cherry, plum, mulberry and sometimes chocolate and liquorice. Tannins are moderate and soft; acidity is surprisingly fresh for a hot-climate grape. It's Sicily's most planted red.

Nero d'Avola keeps good natural acidity even in Sicily's heat, partly because of its genetics and partly because the best vineyards benefit from sea breezes and altitude. It's also called Calabrese, a name that may mean it came from Calabria, or from an old Sicilian dialect word. It was once shipped north to deepen paler wines.
Avola is a town in south-east Sicily, the grape's historic home.

In the glass, look for deep ruby-purple colour, ripe dark fruit, and a juicy, fresh palate with soft tannins. Unoaked versions are fruity and bright; oaked ones show vanilla and spice. The juiciness and freshness, despite the ripe fruit, are the clue.
Nero d'Avola was once shipped north to add colour to paler wines.
Yes. Its deep colour made it a popular blending wine before it became known in its own right.
Nero d'Avola gives dark, ripe fruit with fresh acidity
Its name means the black of Avola; it's also called Calabrese
It's Sicily's most planted red grape
Explain how Sicily's climate shapes it

Nero d'Avola grows all over Sicily, but the south-east, around Avola, Noto, Pachino and Vittoria, is its historic home. Limestone and sandy soils there give fresher, more elegant wines. Inland and western areas produce riper, fuller styles. It's also planted in Australia and California in small amounts.

Sicily is hot and dry, with sea breezes and altitude moderating it. Bush vines, called alberello, are traditional, shading the fruit. Many growers now use trellises. Nero d'Avola needs heat but can lose freshness in the hottest sites, so coastal and hillside vineyards are valued.
Match each Sicilian wine to its grapes.
Nero d'Avola is found across Sicily, but not on Etna.

Sicily's only DOCG, Cerasuolo di Vittoria, blends 50 to 70% Nero d'Avola with Frappato. Nero gives structure and colour; Frappato gives perfume and lightness. The result is a bright, cherry-scented red, lighter than many Sicilian reds. Cerasuolo here means cherry-red.
Cerasuolo di Vittoria blends Nero d'Avola with ____.
Frappato adds perfume and lightness to Nero d'Avola's depth.
Nero d'Avola's historic home is south-east Sicily
Sea breezes and hills keep it fresh
Cerasuolo di Vittoria, Sicily's only DOCG, blends it with Frappato

Nero d'Avola's juicy fruit and fresh acidity suit tomato-based pasta, pizza, grilled sausages and lamb. In Sicily, it goes with pasta alla Norma, made with aubergine, tomato and ricotta salata. Its soft tannins work with tuna or swordfish steaks too.

Serve at 15 to 17 degrees. Most Nero d'Avola is best within three to five years, when fruit is bright. Oaked, concentrated versions from top sites age 10 years or more. Cerasuolo di Vittoria can be served slightly cooler.
Why can Nero d'Avola work with tuna or swordfish?
Its soft tannins don't clash with meaty fish
Soft tannins won't make firm fish taste metallic.
Try a lightly chilled Cerasuolo di Vittoria in summer. Its cherry fruit and freshness work like a light red or a serious rosé.
